title: Failure modes: timeouts, partial failure, cascades, thundering herd
story:
A component that is nearly always fast is not nearly always fast enough, and the arithmetic showing why is the most useful thing in this lesson.

Dean and Barroso set it out in 2013. Suppose one server has a 99th percentile latency of one second — a one in a hundred chance of being slow. A request that fans out to 100 servers and waits for all of them will see that slow response more often than not. Push the fan-out to 2,000 servers and even a one in ten thousand chance of a slow response means 18% of requests exceed one second. The individual components got better and the user experience got worse, because a request depending on many things is exposed to the worst of them rather than the average.

Their framing follows from that: software techniques tolerating latency variability are vital to building responsive large-scale services, by analogy with fault tolerance. Just as fault tolerance creates a reliable whole from less-reliable parts, large online services need to create a predictably responsive whole out of less-predictable parts — which they call latency tail-tolerant. And the conclusion worth arguing with people about: simply stamping out all sources of performance variability will not achieve responsiveness as systems scale up. Variability is a permanent property to be tolerated, not a defect queue to be worked through.

The failures then compose in ways worth naming separately. Partial failure is the distinctive one — a call that neither succeeds nor fails but does not return, which is a state a local function call does not have, and it is why every remote call needs a bound on how long you will wait. Cascades follow: when a dependency slows, its callers hold threads or connections waiting, exhaust their own capacity, and become slow for requests that never touched the original problem. And the thundering herd is the recovery pathology — everything that was waiting retries at the same moment, and the service that just came back is immediately knocked over by the crowd that was queuing for it.

Among the mitigations they describe are hedged requests: send the same request to several replicas, take the first response and cancel the rest. Note the refinement they add, because it is the interesting part. Cancellation messages often arrive after processing has begun, so the naive form adds significant surplus load — the fix is to delay the second request rather than issuing both immediately. That is the shape of every remedy here: you buy latency with load, which is the resource that was already scarce when things were slow.

problem.name: Tail tolerance
problem.shape: A request depends on many components, each nearly always fast, and it is exposed to the worst of them rather than the average.
tell: a request fans out to many services and waits for all of them
median latency is healthy and the high percentiles are not
a slow dependency is making unrelated requests slow
everything retries at once when a service recovers
problem.move: Bound every wait, because a call that never returns is worse than one that fails. Degrade rather than fail where a partial answer is useful. Where latency matters more than load, hedge — but delay the second request rather than issuing both. And make retries jittered and budgeted so recovery does not become the next outage.
problem.invariant: A request that waits on many components inherits their worst case, so end-to-end latency is governed by the tail of each dependency rather than by its median.
problem.breaks: Every mitigation spends the resource that was scarce. Hedging buys latency with load, timeouts convert slow responses into failed ones and abandon work that would have arrived, and retries multiply traffic exactly when the system is least able to serve it.

cost.time: a bounded wait abandons responses that were about to arrive, so some successful work is discarded as the price of predictability
cost.space: duplicate in-flight requests and their queued work at several replicas
cost.beats: waiting indefinitely, which converts one slow dependency into a system-wide outage, and eliminating variability, which does not scale

worked.problem: Why can a service whose slow responses are rare still be slow almost every time?
worked.reasoning:
Because a request that depends on many components is exposed to the worst of them, and rare events stop being rare once you sample enough of them.

The arithmetic is the argument. Take a server with a 99th percentile latency of one second — one request in a hundred is slow. Fan a request out to 100 such servers and wait for all of them, and you will see at least one slow response more often than not. Push the fan-out to 2,000 and even a one in ten thousand chance of slowness means 18% of requests exceed one second.

Sit with the direction of that. Improving the per-server rate from one in a hundred to one in ten thousand is a hundred-fold improvement in the component, and the system still has nearly a fifth of its requests running slow, because the fan-out grew. The component got much better and the experience got worse.

Which is why the conclusion is framed as an analogy to fault tolerance rather than as a performance problem. Just as fault tolerance creates a reliable whole from less-reliable parts, large services need to create a predictably responsive whole from less-predictable parts — tail-tolerant rather than merely fast. And explicitly: simply stamping out all sources of performance variability will not achieve responsiveness as systems scale up. Variability is permanent; the question is what you build on top of it.

So the moves are structural rather than remedial. Reduce what you must wait for — not every fan-out needs every answer, and returning a result from ninety-five of a hundred shards is usually better than waiting for the hundredth. Bound every wait, because unbounded waiting is how one slow dependency becomes a system-wide outage: callers hold threads waiting, exhaust their own capacity, and go slow for requests that never touched the original problem. And where latency matters more than load, hedge — send the same request to several replicas and take the first.

The refinement on hedging is the detail I would make sure to give, because it is where the naive version goes wrong. Cancellation messages often arrive after processing has begun, so simply duplicating every request adds significant surplus load. The fix is to delay the second request — issue it only if the first has not answered within some threshold — which captures most of the benefit for a small fraction of the extra work.

And the general shape: every one of these spends load to buy latency, and load is exactly what was scarce when things were slow. Which is also why retries need jitter and a budget, since the thundering herd is this same trade applied without thinking — everything retrying at once is the system buying latency with load at the precise moment it has none.

problem.practice: Take a request that fans out and count the dependencies it waits for. Look up the 99th percentile of each, and work out how often at least one of them is slow. Then decide which of those answers you could return without.

beats.broke: A component that is nearly always fast is not nearly always fast enough, because a request depending on many components is exposed to the worst of them rather than the average.
beats.fix: Treat variability as a permanent property to be tolerated rather than a defect to be removed — bound every wait, degrade rather than fail, and where latency matters more than load, ask several replicas and take the first answer.
beats.cost: The tolerations cost work: a bounded wait abandons responses that would have arrived, and duplicate requests buy latency with load, which is exactly the resource that was scarce when things were slow.
